topline: Four stories today: a student movement takes power in an EU candidate country, Lula's win keeps the Mercosur deal alive, Brussels unveils new deportation powers for Frontex, and Marine Le Pen opens her 2027 campaign.

stories.title: Student-led list wins Serbia's election as Vučić concedes
stories.summary: The Student List, which grew out of nearly two years of protests after the deadly 2024 Novi Sad station collapse, is projected to win about 135–140 of the 250 seats in Serbia's parliament. Aleksandar Vučić, who has dominated Serbian politics for more than a decade, admitted defeat on election night. Ursula von der Leyen and António Costa congratulated the winners and offered help with rule-of-law and anti-corruption reforms. OSCE observers still reported misuse of state resources and pro-government media bias during the campaign.
stories.why: Serbia is an EU candidate whose accession talks have stalled. A new majority could restart them, though its line on Russia sanctions and Kosovo is still unclear.

left.angle: Told as a democratic victory over a strongman. Coverage centres on the street celebrations, the political newcomers on the list, and Vučić blaming independent media and foreign interference for his loss.

outlets.name: CNN
outlets.note: Frames the race as a right-wing ruling party against a diverse youth movement.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Highlights record turnout and the students' promise of justice and dignity.

right.angle: Welcomes the fall of a Putin-friendly leader but warns Europe not to celebrate too early. It stresses that the Student List opposed sanctions on Russia during the campaign, that Serbia will keep buying Russian gas, and that a new face in power does not always change policy.

outlets.name: The Telegraph
outlets.note: Compares Serbia with Hungary, where it says the new government kept parts of Orbán's anti-Brussels line.

stories.differ: Left-leaning coverage asks whether democracy won. Right-leaning coverage asks whether Russia lost. Neither has much detail yet on what the students will actually do in government.

stories.title: Lula re-elected in Brazil; Brussels relieved over the Mercosur deal
stories.summary: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva won Brazil's run-off with about 51.8% of the vote against far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro, who has not accepted the result. Von der Leyen and Costa were among the first leaders to congratulate him. Brussels had feared that a Bolsonaro presidency would pull Brazil away from the EU–Mercosur trade agreement signed in January.
stories.why: The result keeps the EU's trade deal with South America on track, but the European Parliament still has to approve it.

left.angle: Read as a win for democracy and multilateralism, and as a signal for Europe's left. Spain's Pedro Sánchez linked it directly to his own snap election next month, and progressive figures abroad joined in.

outlets.name: Al Jazeera
outlets.note: Quotes Sánchez: "The global progressive comeback has just begun."

outlets.name: EUobserver
outlets.note: Presents Lula as a democratic ally for the EU on climate and trade.

right.angle: Puts the money and the dispute first. Headlines dwell on Brazilian markets selling off, Bolsonaro taking his defeat to the electoral court, and Brussels officials congratulating Lula.

outlets.name: Brussels Signal
outlets.note: Runs the story under the headline "EU bureaucrats congratulate Lula".

stories.differ: Left-leaning outlets treat Lula's win as a political message for Europe. Right-leaning outlets focus on investors' reaction and Bolsonaro's challenge, and are cooler on the EU's enthusiasm.

stories.title: Commission presents a Frontex overhaul with new deportation powers today
stories.summary: The European Commission unveils its reform of the EU border agency on Tuesday 27 October. According to plans reported by Euronews and Politico Europe, Frontex would be able to help non-EU governments return migrants to their home countries, take part in deportations from return hubs that member states can now set up outside the EU, and deploy to border emergencies within 24 hours. Commissioners Henna Virkkunen and Magnus Brunner are due to present it after the weekly College meeting.
stories.why: It pushes EU migration enforcement further beyond Europe's borders. Member states and the European Parliament will now fight over its scope and oversight.

left.angle: Leads with rights concerns. Researchers describe Frontex turning into a deportation agency that works far from the EU's own borders, NGOs demand stronger oversight, and coverage recalls the agency's past pushback controversies.

outlets.name: Statewatch
outlets.note: Argues the review will widen harmful border practices.

outlets.name: EUobserver
outlets.note: Earlier report on the plan, framing Frontex as controversy-hit.

right.angle: No fresh right-leaning take on today's package yet. Earlier coverage treated tougher returns as overdue: it welcomed the new deportation law as the end of an open-door era and linked the 24-hour rapid response force to this summer's mass crossing at Ceuta.

outlets.name: The European Conservative
outlets.note: June report celebrating the Parliament's deportation law.

outlets.name: Brussels Signal
outlets.note: September report on the rapid reaction force after Ceuta.

stories.differ: Left-leaning coverage asks who will hold Frontex to account. Right-leaning coverage asks whether it will actually send more people back.

stories.title: Marine Le Pen launches her 2027 presidential campaign in Orléans
stories.summary: Le Pen opened her fourth run for the presidency at the National Rally congress in Orléans, promising to "restore the rule of law" after weeks of protests and rioting in French cities. She also pledged capped energy bills, tax cuts and a smaller French contribution to the EU budget. An Ipsos poll puts her at 32–34% in the first round. Thousands marched against the party in Orléans the day before, and an appeals court has upheld her embezzlement conviction.
stories.why: France is the EU's second-largest economy. A Le Pen presidency would change the bloc's budget, migration and Ukraine debates.

left.angle: The story is the siege around the rally: bridges closed, the city centre sealed off, a Sunday protest banned, and reports of journalists being roughed up at the congress. Coverage describes a radical programme presented in an optimistic tone.

outlets.name: Le Monde
outlets.note: Headline speaks of radicalism and optimism in a city under siege. Link goes to the headline listing.

outlets.name: Mediapart
outlets.note: Details the security lockdown and attacks on journalists. Link goes to the headline listing.

right.angle: The story is the speech: Le Pen rejecting national decline and promising a French renaissance, a confident party base, and her poll lead. The conviction appears mainly as something her supporters shrug off.

outlets.name: Europe 1
outlets.note: Headline: Le Pen refuses fatalism and promises France's rebirth. Link goes to the headline listing.

outlets.name: Le Figaro
outlets.note: Focuses on how she has reorganised the party around her campaign. Link goes to the headline listing.

stories.differ: Left-leaning papers report what happened around the rally. Right-leaning outlets report what was said inside it.
